The fundraiser brought 96 paying participants to Rolling Green Golf Club in Springfield, Pennsylvania. The money will support youth programs for underserved and underrepresented children across Philadelphia.The event gave the Kelces another way to support their adopted city. Be Philly, which Jason and Kylie founded in 2022, backs programs that give young people access to mentorship, academic help, career guidance and new opportunities. The foundation now has its largest group of grantees yet.The June 1 fundraiser mixed charity with the kind of fun that has become familiar around Jason Kelce. Former Eagles player Brent Celek, former Flyers Scott Hartnell and Sean Couturier, and former Villanova basketball coach Jay Wright joined the golfers.Jason also brought some classic Philly energy to the course. He invited well-known Eagles fans to heckle golfers at the 10th hole. A mariachi band played near the 14th green while an Elvis impersonator moved around the course in a golf cart.The jokes had a purpose beyond entertainment. The event raised $553,500 through participant fees and sponsorships for Be Philly.Jason spoke about the foundation during the evening portion of the event. He pointed to Philadelphia's struggles with economic mobility and explained why the city remains so important to him.“Everything that I’ve had in my career and everything I’m having post-career was built because of this city and the people who have supported me and our team,” Jason told Philadelphia Magazine at the June 1 golf outing.That connection sits at the heart of Be Philly's work.The foundation does not simply hand out money without a larger plan. Be Philly supports existing youth programs that already work with children in Philadelphia.In 2026, the foundation has eight grantee organizations. Their work covers areas such as youth sports, mentorship, education and support for young people facing difficult circumstances.One example is Safe-Hub's youth soccer program in Kensington. Another is Valley Youth House, which helps young people dealing with housing instability and homelessness.The foundation also supports Coded by. According to *Philadelphia Magazine*, the organization grew from serving about 350 young people each year to more than 1,200 after developing its relationship with Be Philly.That growth shows where the Kelces want their money to go. The goal is not simply to attach their names to a fundraiser. They are putting money behind programs that already work with Philadelphia children and helping those groups reach more young people.The foundation also has bigger plans ahead. Be Philly expects to distribute more than $1 million in total funds during 2026. It plans to increase its annual grant-making budget to around $500,000 by 2027. The foundation also plans to add a second grant cycle each year.For Jason and Kylie, the $553,500 raised on June 1 is another step in that plan. The golf outing lasted one day, but the money raised there can keep moving through Philadelphia youth programs long after the golfers left Rolling Green Golf Club.That gives the Kelces' latest charity effort a clear purpose. Their growing Be Philly Foundation is putting more resources behind the young people and community programs they want to see thrive across Philadelphia.

Sourav Ganguly has said there is no conflict of interest in his taking charge as head coach of IPL franchise Delhi Capitals while continuing as president of the Cricket Association of Bengal (CAB), saying he has the order of the BCCI ombudsman.Ganguly will take charge of an IPL team as head coach for the first time after replacing Hemang Badani at Delhi Capitals ahead of the 2027 season.The former India captain has been associated with the Capitals since 2019 and has held several roles, including Director of Cricket for both the men's and women's teams. I'm looking forward to it," Ganguly told reporters on Tuesday, as quoted by news agency PTI.Ganguly was speaking after watching India's 1-6 defeat against Uruguay in a FIFA international friendly at the Salt Lake Stadium.Asked about the potential conflict of interest arising from his dual roles, Ganguly said: "I've got the order of ombudsman."Ganguly also backed India's decision to play against top international teams, saying the exposure would help Indian footballers improve."It's a good initiative and they will learn in this way. It (the development) doesn't happen overnight.You only improve playing against good teams," he said.India had earlier drawn 1-1 against Panama in Bengaluru before losing to five-time world champions Brazil 0-4 and two-time world champions Uruguay 1-6 in back-to-back matches.Ganguly, who represented India in 113 tests and 311 one-day internationals, made his coaching debut last year at Pretoria Capitals in the South African SA20 league. On November 22, 2022, Bhuvneshwar Kumar played his last match for India, against New Zealand. Four years later, he has returned to the Indian T20I squad against the same opposition.The recall came on earlier this week, when the BCCI announced India's squad for the five-match T20I series in New Zealand. The 36-year-old’s name was one of the biggest talking points in the 16-member squad.In between were four years without an India call-up, a shift from international regular to domestic leader, and a fitness routine that, according to the man who has worked closely with him, demanded hours every day.A few months before his return, he had taken 28 wickets in 16 matches for Royal Challengers Bengaluru in IPL 2026, finishing as the joint-highest wicket-taker of the season. His wickets came at an average of 17.89 and an economy rate of 7.95 as RCB won their second successive IPL title.After the IPL, Bhuvneshwar captained Lucknow Falcons in the UPT20 league to the final, taking 14 wickets in 11 matches at 16.57, with an economy rate of 6.82.After RCB made it to their back-to-back final of IPL, TimesofIndia.com spoke to Bhuvneshwar's personal strength and conditioning coach, Surya Pratap Yadav, about the changes behind the scenes. One of the biggest areas of focus was body composition. “Our primary focus has been reducing body fat while increasing muscle mass. As athletes age, muscle loss becomes a concern, so we worked extensively on strength training, protein intake, and supplementation.“Bhuvneshwar's body fat percentage has come down from 19% to 14%, while maintaining his weight, which indicates muscle gain. His strength levels have improved significantly, and that has helped increase force production and running speed,” Surya Pratap had told TimesofIndia.com in May this year.“Discipline is the biggest factor. He understands his body's weak points and works on them proactively. We dedicate nearly an hour every day to rehab and injury-prevention exercises. Along with that, we focus heavily on recovery, hydration, sleep, protein intake, and supplements. All of these factors help him stay fit throughout the season,” added Pratap.“A lot more than people realise, he spends 6-7 hours a day training. That includes gym sessions, rehabilitation work, recovery routines, batting practice, bowling practice, and training in different environments. Even if it isn't always visible on social media, the amount of effort he puts in every day is tremendous,” Surya Pratap Yadav had said.For a fast bowler in his mid-30s, that workload has to be managed as carefully as the bowling itself. Bhuvneshwar's answer was to make the routine part of his cricket life rather than something reserved for a comeback attempt.The years after his India exit were not spent away from competitive cricket. Bhuvneshwar remained a key figure for Uttar Pradesh in domestic cricket, leading the bowling attack in competitions including the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy and Vijay Hazare Trophy. The IPL remained another constant.He had already stopped attaching his daily work to the expectation of a national recall, but the grind continued. In a video posted by RCB, Bhuvneshwar explained why he had stopped setting long-term targets.“I am not thinking about India’s comeback. It has been many years since I stopped keeping or making long-term goals because whenever I did that, it never worked for me. I am happy that I have played 200 matches and taken so many wickets in the powerplay and at the death. I think it is all a reward for what I have done over the years.Bhuvneshwar's return for the NZ series also puts his bowling in a wider context. He has long been one of India's most effective swing bowlers, particularly when the new ball offers movement. His overseas record has included strong spells in England, the West Indies, South Africa and other conditions where the ability to move the ball in the air remains valuable.However, his returns in New Zealand have been modest - having taken 15 wickets in 15 matches, with an average of 38.00. His numbers on the last New Zealand trip: four wickets in five T20Is at an average of 40.00 and an economy rate of 8.42.But the relevance of Bhuvneshwar's return is not confined to the numbers from one series. His new-ball swing gives India another type of option, particularly as the team looks towards conditions in New Zealand.The comeback also attracted attention from former India players. Suresh Raina called the selection ‘thoroughly deserved’, while Kris Srikkanth described it as a ‘fantastic move’. Virender Sehwag questioned whether age should be a deciding factor if a 35- or 36-year-old fast bowler is still producing match-winning performances. Mohammad Kaif has also pointed to Bhuvneshwar's ability to trouble batters with movement.
Article Summary: Bhuvneshwar Kumar has been recalled to India's T20 squad. The 36-year-old has not played for India since November 22, 2022. He has taken 28 wickets in 16 matches for Royal Challengers Bengaluru in IPL 2026.

Article Title: Satya Niketan back to routine, but tremors bring back safety scare
Article Text: New Delhi: A month after a building collapse in Satya Niketan left students worried about the safety of their accommodation, reports of tremors across the city Tuesday night briefly revived those fears. Although the initial alarm soon gave way to relief, for students living in the area’s tightly packed paying guest accommodations and rented rooms, even mild tremors were enough to trigger the memories of the collapse.The episode briefly brought the question of building safety back into focus in a neighbourhood where academic schedules, rent agreements and proximity to colleges make moving out difficult. On Tuesday night, many residents came out onto narrow lanes. “I rushed downstairs. A few other students had already come out, and we stood outside for some time,” said Rahul , a third-year student of Delhi University. “After what happened here last month, the first thought was whether the building was safe.”Meenal, a student of Atma Ram Sanatan Dharma College, said students in lanes 2 and 3 stepped outside. “There is still a lot of fear,” she said. At the same time, she added, repeated concerns over safety have meant that some residents are gradually becoming desensitised to the risks around them.For women students, the tremors revived a different worry: whether they would be able to get out of their PGs quickly in an emergency.Meenal said several girls’ PGs enforced strict night-time curfews. Recalling an earlier earthquake, she said a friend living in a PG had wanted to step outside after feeling tremors but was allegedly told by the warden that the gate could not be opened because she did not have the keys. “Girls were restricted inside the buildings because of their curfew timings. How unsafe is that in times of emergency?” Meenal said.The building collapse in Satya Niketan, a congested student hub adjoining DU’s South Campus, had claimed seven lives and raised concerns over the condition and structural safety of buildings in the area.For some students, the immediate instinct after the collapse was to leave. Meenal, whose parents live in Noida, was at home when the building came down. She said her parents were reluctant to let her return to Satya Niketan. Others shifted out temporarily. Hitesh, a Sri Venkateswara College student from Bihar, said he spent nearly a month at a friend’s PG because he did not want to live alone immediately. His parents, too, had urged him to return home.But leaving Satya Niketan permanently has proved more complicated. Hitesh said many tenants were bound by rental agreements with lock-in periods that could extend up to 11 months. The collapse also came in the middle of the academic session, making an immediate shift impractical. For now, he has returned, but plans to look for another area next semester.Himadri from Maitreyi College faces a similar dilemma. She has considered moving out, but shifting midway through the session has not been easy.For Shagun, whose parents live in Indore, proximity to college ultimately outweighed the unease. “There is no option but to stay here as this is closer to our colleges,” she said. Her own PG, she added, appeared to be in a relatively better condition, giving her enough reassurance to continue staying there.A month on, the student neighbourhood has largely slipped back into its familiar routine. But Tuesday night was a reminder that while daily life may have resumed, the unease over the buildings they call home has not entirely gone away.
Article Summary: Reports of tremors across the city Tuesday night briefly revived those fears. The episode briefly brought the question of building safety back into focus in a neighbourhood where academic schedules, rent agreements and proximity to colleges make moving out difficult. For women students, the tremors revived a different worry: whether they would be able to get out of their PGs quickly in an emergency.

Article Title: From idol-making to dhunuchi naach: Walking through Delhi’s Durga Puja story
Article Text:
The idea of starting this pre-Pujo walk, back in 2013, was to break down a cultural barrier , says DBF co-founder Ramit Mitra

Ramit's walk began at the footsteps leading to the Kali Mandir in CR Park

Mythology to making of idols: Walks give the back story to Durga Puja

The walk is an experience to soak the puja buzz that takes over CR Park during this time of year. The idea of starting this walk, back in 2013, was to break down a cultural barrier Ramit Mitra

Beyond the pandal: The people and craft behind pujo

Archana Jain with the group of participants during the walk

​‘Documenting the making of the idols is a complete photo story’​

We usually see the finished idol and the grandeur of the pandal, but rarely think about the artisans and the generations of skill that go into creating the goddess Archana Jain

A puchka stop added a tasty detour to the walk

puja

While crossing the alleys of CR Park markets, the group takes pit stops at shops to catch glimpses of the groceries and vegetables used in Bengali households, Puja decor and more.





As Delhi gears up for Durga Puja, pre-pujo walks are taking participants beyond pandal-hopping to explore the history, traditions and people behind the festival. In CR Park, the Pujo Aschey walk by DelhiByFoot and the Mitti Se Maa Ka Safar walk by O’Pause Travel Experiences, in collaboration with Sabhyata Heritage Walks, offered different routes into the neighbourhood’s pujo story – from its Bengali roots and the mythology of Durga to the rituals and craft behind idol-making.At 8am, around 20 people gathered outside Market 4 in CR Park recently for DelhiByFoot founder Ramit Mitra’s Pujo Aschey walk, including a self-described “pseudo-Bengali” and a non-Bengali who had grown up around pujo, both curious about the history, rituals and people behind the celebration.On the steps leading to Kali Bari Mandir, Ramit began by talking about the formation of the East Pakistan Displaced Persons (EPDP) Colony (now called Chittaranjan Park, or CR Park) in 1967, sharing, “In 1970, CR Park’s first, and Delhi’s second, puja took place... CR Park hosts 12 pujas now, with several cultural competitions and events taking place before and during the puja. It is considered the best way to stay connected to Bengali roots. ”Ramit began with the mythology of Durga and Mahishasura before turning to the making of the pratima. At two murtikar workshops – one at Kali Bari and another behind Chandralok Cinema – participants saw the stages of idol-making and learnt about the rituals and traditions behind it.For Virendra Shekhawat, founder of Delhi Photography Club, photo walks at the murtikar workshops present a complete photo story. “What makes idol-making fascinating from a photographer’s perspective is that you can capture the entire process as one complete photo story — from sourcing and preparing the soil to building the structure, shaping the idol, drying it, painting it and finally seeing it immersed. You see something take shape from the soil, become a fully formed idol, and then eventually return to nature. ”For Granthika Chatterjee, who grew up in Kolkata, the visit to the murtikar workshops brought back memories of her childhood. “For 18 years, it was a ritual for my father and me to visit Kumartuli (in Kolkata) and simply absorb the atmosphere. We were like those who are called pujo pagol. Coming here brought back that nostalgia.”The Mitti Se Maa Ka Safar walk, led by Archana Jain of O’Pause Travel Experiences in collaboration with Sabhyata Heritage Walks, began at Kali Mandir at 5pm recently. Archana traced the lesser-known history of the displaced Bengali community, stopping at Market No 1 to savour puchkas while discussing the early community Durga Puja. At the murtikar workshop behind Chandralok Cinema, she explained the rituals from Mahalaya to Dashami, including Bodhon, the awakening of the goddess.Conducting the walk for the second time, Jain explored CR Park through its craft traditions. “For me, the most interesting part is understanding how a displaced community rebuilt not just homes, but an entire cultural world in a new city. The Durga Puja we see today is also a story of migration, memory, identity and belonging. One of the most fascinating parts of the walk is watching the making of the Durga idol. I call it the ‘Kumartuli of CR Park’ because it gives people a glimpse of the craft and labour behind the celebration. We usually see the finished idol and the grandeur of the pandal, but rarely think about the artisans and the generations of skill that go into creating the goddess.”Mona Suri Mathur, a resident of Indirapuram, saw the walk as an opportunity to explore community and new experiences beyond midlife. “During the pre-pujo walk, there were several references to the importance of community. Walks like this are just the kind of experiences one looks for at this stage of life – beyond midlife,” she said.Smriti Pandey, who previously lived in CR Park, revisited memories of pandal-hopping in the neighbourhood. “I am reminiscing about the old days, when I used to stay in the area and had a gala time hopping from one pandal to another. Through this walk, I witnessed a different side of pujo,” she said.For Nikita Ahuja, who studied at a Bengali school and has long attended Minto Road Puja, the walk connected the dots, offering a glimpse into the people and processes behind the celebrations. “What I took away from the walk was how many hundreds and thousands of people are involved in making eachhappen.”
Article Summary: Pujo Aschey walk by DelhiByFoot and Mitti Se Maa Ka Safar walk by O’Pause Travel Experiences, in collaboration with Sabhyata Heritage Walks, offer different routes into the neighbourhood’s pujo story. Walks give the back story to Durga Puja.

Duration: Two hours

Language: Hindi

Should you watch it?

Catch the play at

Prithvi Theatre

on Oct 8 at 8pm and Oct 9 at 6 pm and 9 pm





There are stories in Indian history that have survived not because they found their way into textbooks, but because generations kept telling them. Theatre, film, and television actor, director, Preeta Mathur Thakur’s play attempts to bring one such story out of the shadows; that of Abbakka of Ullala, the 16th-century coastal Karnataka queen who resisted Portuguese expansion and refused to surrender control of her kingdom and its maritime trade.Written-directed by Preeta, with dialogues by Richa Sharad, the two-hour play is an ambitious undertaking, bringing together a large ensemble, elaborate sets, music, and movement. What makes Veera Rani Abbakka Chowtha's story particularly fascinating is that her resistance was not simply about winning a war, but about the fact that as a queen, she understood the larger danger behind the Portuguese presence on the coast. She saw through that what began as trade and promises of protection, could eventually become political control. And so, to protect Ullala’s sovereignty, she built a strong naval force, forged alliances, to challenge the Portuguese monopoly over the spice trade.Preeta's play takes this larger political conflict and places a woman at its centre — not as a symbolic figurehead, but as a ruler making difficult strategic choices, when she is surrounded by men who either underestimate her, oppose her or attempt to use her political circumstances to their advantage.The production’s biggest strength is its scale. With nearly 26 actors, it has the canvas of an epic, and the stage is aptly designed by the veteran thespian Atul Tiwari.The two narrators using Yakshagana-inspired costumes and movement to introduce, explain and propel the story are an interesting theatrical device, particularly because the play is in Hindi while the legend itself has been preserved through Kannada oral traditions and folk performance.The sheer ambition of the production, however, works against the intimacy that historical storytelling needs. With a large cast, multiple characters, political developments, battles and shifts in location, there is a lot for the audience to absorb. A tighter dramatic focus on Abbakka’s inner conflict -- the woman behind the warrior and ruler -- could make the emotional stakes even stronger.Yes, particularly if you enjoy historical theatre, ensemble productions and stories about lesser-known figures from India’s past.
Article Summary: Preeta Mathur Thakur’s play attempts to bring one such story out of the shadows. Abbakka of Ullala was the 16th-century coastal Karnataka queen who resisted Portuguese expansion. The two-hour play is an ambitious undertaking, bringing together a large ensemble, elaborate sets, music and movement.

Article Title: No frisking, fresh answer book if caught cheating, bags allowed in exam building: IIT-Bombay’s new interim SOP for October 10-11 tests
Article Text:
IIT-Bombay has introduced interim rules for handling suspected cheating during mid-semester examinations on October 10 and 11 (Sahil, wearing what appears to be a black T-shirt and light-coloured trousers, is seen seated on the first bench in the middle of the hall.)

Two forms to record suspected cheating

Counsellors to be alerted if cheating or stress is noticed

July policy had added semester suspension

No security frisking before exams

Bags allowed inside exam building





MUMBAI: No frisking, a fresh answer book if a student is caught allegedly cheating, and an immediate counsellor alert are among the key provisions of IIT-Bombay’s interim procedure for handling suspected academic misconduct during the pending mid-semester examinations on October 10 and 11.The institute’s Senate, at an emergency meeting on Wednesday, put its July 2026 rules on penalties for academic misconduct on hold and decided to revert to the milder April 2015 policy for the two examinations. Under the interim arrangement, faculty members can record suspected dishonesty in a prescribed form, while students will have the option of submitting their own written account on a separate form.The revision comes in the wake of the death by suicide of second-year BTech student Sahil Wakode, who was allegedly found copying by an invigilator. IIT-Bombay had subsequently postponed examinations scheduled for September 26 and 27 after faculty members sought a clear standard operating procedure for dealing with suspected malpractice.Under the new interim procedure, two separate forms will be used when cheating is suspected. One will be completed by the faculty member, while the student may optionally submit a written account of their version of events.The case will subsequently be placed before the departmental disciplinary action committee (DDAC), which will decide how it should proceed. Faculty members and students may be required to appear before the committee and provide additional information.The DDAC will meet only a week after the entire examination season concludes.A source said the forms were intended only to collect information and did not amount to the filing of charges against a student. The final decision would rest with the disciplinary committee.Wednesday’s meeting was opened to all faculty members, beyond the Senate’s membership, to seek suggestions on the interim procedure.According to the interim rules report, a copy of which is with TOI, faculty members who suspect cheating or notice signs of stress in a student must alert a quick response team (QRT) of counsellors.The objective is to provide immediate support while minimising disturbance to the student concerned and others appearing for the examination.Invigilators have been instructed to collect unauthorised material, including chits, phones, electronic devices and answer papers, with minimal conversation and disruption. They may photograph material that has to be returned, such as a phone. If there is a doubt about a student’s identity, the invigilator may also photograph the student at their desk.The original answer book will be collected, but the student will be allowed to continue writing the examination in a fresh answer book for the remaining time.After the examination, the invigilator may complete the prescribed form and offer the student an opportunity to record their version at a designated venue in the presence of additional staff.The signed faculty form, collected material, original answer book and the student’s form, if submitted, will then be handed over to the head of the department conducting the course.Digital material may be emailed, while phones will be returned after the examination. Students will have to acknowledge receipt of their phones by signing the form.The QRT helpline must be alerted for counselling whenever a student leaves the examination hall.Under the April 2015 guidelines, using a mobile phone during an examination attracted an FR (fail-repeat) grade. The July 2026 policy had added a semester-long suspension.Sources said the suspension would not apply to a first offence under the interim arrangement. Repeat offences, however, would attract suspension.Use of phones, chits, books or other unauthorised material during toilet or bio-breaks would continue to attract an FR grade and a semester suspension.Security guards will no longer frisk students before examinations under the interim procedure.Faculty members had questioned searches resembling airport-style security checks, saying they could create an impression that every student was being treated as a “suspect”.“We want to convey we trust our students, though we will verify by doing thorough invigilation,” said a faculty member.Another source said an invigilator who suspected a student could call a counsellor and ask the student to empty their pockets.The report also states that disciplinary proceedings must give students a fair opportunity to present their viewpoint before the departmental committee. Students will also have the right to appeal before an institute committee.Disciplinary action will follow if unauthorised practices are established.Sources said the new arrangement would “ease the burden on faculty handling suspected cheating”, with professional counsellors providing support. The disciplinary committee, however, will determine the outcome of each case.The drafting committee comprised Profs Suvarn Kulkarni, Pratibha Sharma, Varsha Apte and Amitava De, along with four student representatives. Sources said the group spent about 30 hours preparing the interim procedure.Clear instructions will be shared with invigilators before the weekend examinations, a source said.Students may also now bring bags into the examination building, reversing the earlier restriction, but they will have to leave them outside the examination hall.The report states that the institute's objective is to “create an environment conducive to quality teaching and learning while maintaining assessment integrity”. Its default assumption is that students are committed to learning and following examination rules.As per the academic calendar approved by the Senate, end-semester examinations are scheduled over 13 days from November 10 to 21 and will also be held on Saturdays and Sundays.
Article Summary: IIT-Bombay has introduced interim rules for handling suspected cheating during mid-semester examinations on October 10 and 11. No frisking, a fresh answer book if a student is caught allegedly cheating, and an immediate counsellor alert are among the key provisions. The revision comes in the wake of the death by suicide of second-year BTech student Sahil Wakode.

Article Title: ​Two fined for water wastage in Sambhajinagar; Action begins before Oct 15 deadline
Article Text:
Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar

:





As drought threatens to deepen the city’s water crisis, the civic body has begun cracking down on wastage ahead of its Oct 15 deadline to repair leaking taps and pipelines. Two residents were fined, and 33 illegal water connections snapped on Tuesday.The Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar Municipal Corporation (CSMC) has asked citizens to fix leaking taps, domestic connections and internal pipelines by Oct 15. However, municipal commissioner Amol Yedge has ordered field action already as the civic body looks to conserve every drop in a drought year.During patrols in Aref Colony and Hilal Colony, water supply department teams spotted two residents wasting tap water. One was fined Rs 10,000 for allowing water to flow onto the road. Another was fined Rs 5,000 for failing to repair a tap and allowing water to go waste.“We once again appeal to citizens to close taps after filling and ensure water does not flow into drains or roads. It is our collective responsibility to save water during the current drought situation, failing which the water crisis could aggravate further,” Yedge said.After Oct 15, the corporation will impose a graded penalty for water wastage. A first violation will attract a Rs 5,000 fine and a second Rs 10,000. A third violation will invite a Rs 25,000 penalty along with a criminal case.The civic body has also turned its attention to water theft.On Tuesday, a special squad disconnected 33 illegal water connections in Nagsen Colony, Roshan Gate and Asifiya Colony. The team found unauthorised connections tapped into a 200mm main pipeline. These were also causing heavy leakage, apart from water theft.CSMC has warned that illegal connections will not be tolerated. It plans to intensify the drive across the city.
Article Summary: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar Municipal Corporation (CSMC) has asked citizens to fix leaking taps, domestic connections and internal pipelines by Oct 15. Two residents were fined, and 33 illegal water connections snapped on Tuesday. A first violation will attract a Rs 5,000 fine and a second Rs 10,000.

Article Title: Independents in fray may invite trouble for candidates of major parties
Article Text:
Kolhapur:





At least 56 independents for graduates’ constituency and 39 for teachers’ constituency have filed their nominations for Pune division MLC seats. If not convinced to withdraw these candidates stir up trouble for candidates of major political parties by dividing the vote share.Meanwhile, BJP and Shiv Sena still have not reached a decision on whether to withdraw nomination or have a friendly fight for the teachers’ constituency. BJP has nominated Kaustubh Gavde and Shiv Sena has nominated Mangesh Chivate. For the graduates’ seat, Shiv Sena (UBT)’s Sunil Modi, NCP (SP)’s Harshada Jadhav and BJP’s Smita Jadhav have filed the nomination.The last day for withdrawal of the nomination is Friday up to 3pm.“There will be meeting of Mahavikas Aghadi netas on Wednesday. One of our MVA partner has fielded their candidate for Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar against Shiv Sena (UBT). If there the candidate withdraws then I will withdraw my candidature and support MVA’s candidate,” said Sunil Modi.Mangesh Chivate has begun his campaign. The constituency has five districts and 50,000 voters. He addressed voters at Phaltan. Ramraje Naik Nimbalkar, former chairman of the legislative council, endorsed Chivate’s candidature, stating that on the one hand education moguls are contesting and on the other hand, Chivate, who comes from a humble background, is trying to make his mark.CM Devendra Fadnavis had said since consensus could not be arrived at both parties have decided to nominate their candidates. Another round of discussion would be held to pitch a consensual candidate.“I have a nomination filed as an independent in case I am asked to step aside. I will contest come what may,” said Chivate, who is promising teachers cashless insurance, old pension and resignation if the promises are not fulfilled within a year of becoming MLC. He also vowed not to take a salary as an MLC till these promises are fulfilled.
Article Summary: At least 56 independents have filed their nominations for Pune division MLC seats. If not convinced to withdraw these candidates stir up trouble for candidates of major political parties. BJP and Shiv Sena still have not reached a decision on whether to withdraw nomination or have a friendly fight for the teachers’ constituency.

Article Title: Mumbai-bound traffic hit after hatchback catches fire on Vashi Creek bridge
Article Text:
The driver immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine.





NAVI MUMBAI: Vehicular traffic from Navi Mumbai towards Mumbai was disrupted for around 30 minutes after a hatchback caught fire while crossing the Vashi Creek Bridge on Friday at around 7.30pm.The driver escaped unhurt. He immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine. However, the fire soon engulfed the entire vehicle, leaving it completely charred.Vashi traffic police alerted the Vashi fire brigade, which reached the spot within 15 minutes. The charred vehicle was later towed away by a crane, following which traffic movement returned to normal.Sunil Kadam, senior inspector of the Vashi traffic unit, said the driver was identified as Sumit Bhikaji Kadam.“At around 7.45pm, we received a call from one Rahul, whose full name is not known, informing us that a car had caught fire on the Mumbai-bound lane of the Vashi Creek Bridge,” said AV Sisode, the on-duty fireman at Vashi fire station.“In the meantime, we also received a call from the Vashi traffic police and immediately rushed to the spot with a fire tender. The Mumbai fire brigade team had also reached the spot as there was some confusion over the jurisdiction,” Sisode said.The fire was subsequently extinguished, and the Vashi fire brigade team returned to the station at around 8.30pm.
Article Summary: The driver immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine. The fire soon engulfed the entire vehicle, leaving it completely charred. The charred vehicle was later towed away by a crane, following which traffic movement returned to normal.
